summary: Nahum 1 opens as a revelation about Nineveh and a vision attributed to Nahum the Elkoshite. The chapter first portrays Yahweh as patient, powerful, and terrifying in judgment, yet good as a refuge for those who trust him. It then turns toward enemies who plot against Yahweh, announces the breaking of oppression, and ends with good news for Judah.
whyItMatters: This chapter sets the book’s main tension: the fall of a violent power is described as both judgment and relief. It also warns readers to track changing addressees, because the same chapter speaks about Nineveh, enemies, an oppressor, and Judah.

context.author: The heading attributes the vision to Nahum the Elkoshite; the book gives no biography and does not identify who arranged the book in its final form.
context.audience: Judah is directly addressed with good news, while Nineveh and Assyrian power are the main targets of the poems.
context.date: Commonly set in the seventh century BCE, between the sack of Thebes in 663 BCE and the fall of Nineveh in 612 BCE, though the book gives no exact date for composition or final arrangement.
context.setting: Judah and the Assyrian imperial world, especially Nineveh, the Assyrian capital in northern Mesopotamia.
context.literaryForm: Prophetic poetry with a heading, a hymn-like opening, direct address, rhetorical questions, threats, assurances, and quoted divine speech.

outline.heading: The vision introduced
outline.note: The chapter begins by naming the subject, Nineveh, and the figure associated with the vision, Nahum the Elkoshite.

outline.heading: Yahweh’s wrath, patience, and power
outline.note: The poem describes Yahweh as avenging and wrathful, yet slow to anger, and pictures sea, rivers, mountains, hills, earth, and rocks overwhelmed before him.

outline.heading: Refuge and full end
outline.note: The chapter holds together Yahweh’s goodness toward those who take refuge in him and his pursuit of enemies into darkness.

outline.heading: Plots brought to nothing
outline.note: Those who plot against Yahweh are pictured as thorns, drunken people, and dry stubble consumed completely.

outline.heading: Affliction ended and bonds broken
outline.note: A divine saying announces that even a strong and numerous enemy will pass away, and that the yoke and bonds on the afflicted will be broken.

outline.heading: Name cut off, Judah called to peace
outline.note: The chapter closes with a command concerning the oppressor’s name, gods, images, and grave, followed by a peace announcement to Judah.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh is slow to anger, and great in power, and will by no means leave the guilty unpunished. Yahweh has his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet.
keyVerses.why: This verse keeps patience, power, and judgment together, which is essential for reading the chapter’s opening portrait of Yahweh.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble; and he knows those who take refuge in him.
keyVerses.why: This verse is the chapter’s clearest statement of refuge, placed in the middle of language about wrath and overwhelming judgment.

keyVerses.text: Now I will break his yoke from off you, and will burst your bonds apart.”
keyVerses.why: This line states the chapter’s promise of release from domination, even though the pronouns require careful reading.

keyVerses.text: Behold, on the mountains the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace! Keep your feasts, Judah! Perform your vows, for the wicked one will no more pass through you. He is utterly cut off.
keyVerses.why: The final verse names Judah and turns the downfall of the wicked one into an announcement of peace and restored worship.

themes: Refuge in the day of trouble

questions.question: What is this chapter about from the first verse?
questions.answer: The opening heading identifies the book as a revelation about Nineveh and a vision attributed to Nahum the Elkoshite. Nineveh is the subject of the poems, while Nahum is the figure named in the heading. The verse gives no biography or account of how the book reached its final form.

questions.question: Why does the chapter describe Yahweh as jealous and avenging?
questions.answer: Verse 2 introduces Yahweh as one who avenges and maintains wrath against adversaries and enemies. In the chapter itself, this language is directed toward those who oppose Yahweh and plot evil, not presented as random anger. Verse 3 immediately adds that Yahweh is slow to anger, so the opening combines wrath, patience, power, and refusal to leave guilt unaddressed.

questions.question: What does “slow to anger” mean here?
questions.answer: Slow to anger describes patience rather than a hasty outburst. In the same verse, Yahweh is great in power and refuses to leave guilt unpunished. The opening holds patience and judgment together; neither description cancels the other.

questions.question: Are the storm, sea, mountains, and rocks literal events in this chapter?
questions.answer: The chapter uses creation imagery to portray overwhelming divine power: Yahweh has his way in storm, rebukes the sea, dries rivers, and makes mountains quake. The text does not give a dated report of a particular storm, earthquake, or river event. Its immediate function is poetic description of power and judgment.

questions.question: How can the chapter say Yahweh is good while also describing wrath?
questions.answer: Verse 7 says Yahweh is good, a stronghold, and knows those who take refuge in him. That statement sits between descriptions of wrath and enemies being pursued into darkness. The chapter distinguishes refuge for those who take refuge from judgment on adversaries; it does not flatten both groups into the same outcome.

questions.question: Who is the “you” in this chapter?
questions.answer: The addressee changes, and not every pronoun is equally clear. Nineveh is named in verse 1, enemies are described in verses 8-10, one who counsels wickedness appears in verse 11, and Judah is named directly in verse 15. Readers should use those anchors rather than assuming every “you” names the same person or group.

questions.question: What are the thorns, drink, and dry stubble doing in verse 10?
questions.answer: Verse 10 uses images of entanglement, drunkenness, and dry stubble to describe how completely the opponents are consumed. The point is vulnerability and total collapse, not a detailed account of one battle tactic. The verse belongs with the surrounding claim that plots against Yahweh will not succeed.

questions.question: What does the broken yoke mean?
questions.answer: The yoke and bonds picture imposed domination. Verses 12–13 announce that a powerful, numerous enemy will pass away and the afflicted people will be released. The promise of broken bonds leads toward the good news addressed explicitly to Judah at the chapter’s close.

questions.question: Why does the ending tell Judah to keep feasts and perform vows?
questions.answer: Verse 15 addresses Judah with good news and peace. Keeping feasts and fulfilling vows picture worship freed from the threat of the wicked one passing through again. In Brenton, most of this verse appears at 2:1, with its closing thought at the beginning of 2:2; compare the wording when switching editions.

glossary.def: An unveiling or message presented here as concerning Nineveh; the chapter itself calls this revelation part of Nahum’s vision.
The city named as the subject of the revelation; in the book setting, it is the Assyrian capital and the main target of the poems.
A place of protection; verse 7 uses the word to describe Yahweh as refuge in a day of trouble.
An image of imposed burden or domination; verse 13 says it will be broken from off the afflicted addressee.
The people directly addressed in verse 15 with good news, peace, feasts, and vows.
